title: Charcot-Marie-Tooth disease: defective myelin protein
vignette: A 15-year-old boy is evaluated for progressive lower extremity weakness. The patient has had difficulty running and keeping up with peers for the past several years and has sprained his ankles on multiple occasions. His father also experienced similar symptoms beginning at the same age and became wheelchair bound. Physical examination shows weakness and atrophy of the distal lower extremity muscles. There is bilateral pes cavus deformity. Ankle reflexes are absent, and sensation to vibration is also absent in the feet. Abnormal function of which of the following is the most likely cause of this patient's condition?

clues.text: His father also experienced similar symptoms beginning at the same age
clues.note: A parent affected at the same age indicates autosomal dominant inheritance - Charcot-Marie-Tooth (CMT1) is classically autosomal dominant (PMP22).

clues.text: weakness and atrophy of the distal lower extremity muscles
clues.note: Length-dependent DISTAL muscle wasting/weakness (feet/legs first) is characteristic of a hereditary peripheral neuropathy like CMT.
Pes cavus (high arches) and hammertoes from chronic imbalance of foot muscles are hallmark skeletal signs of CMT.

clues.text: Ankle reflexes are absent, and sensation to vibration is also absent in the feet
clues.note: Areflexia plus distal sensory loss (vibration) confirm a peripheral neuropathy affecting both motor and sensory nerves.

whatMatters: An adolescent with autosomal dominant, length-dependent distal weakness/atrophy, pes cavus, areflexia, and sensory loss = Charcot-Marie-Tooth disease (CMT), a hereditary peripheral neuropathy. The most common form (CMT1) is caused by a defect in a peripheral MYELIN PROTEIN (PMP22). Answer B (myelin protein).
strategy: Recognize CMT from the tetrad (distal atrophy, pes cavus, areflexia, sensory loss) with dominant family history, then recall its molecular basis: mutations in peripheral nerve MYELIN proteins (e.g., PMP22 in CMT1). Reject dystrophin (Duchenne/Becker - X-linked, pseudohypertrophy), ryanodine receptor (malignant hyperthermia), synaptic vesicle/SNARE (botulism), and tau (neurodegenerative dementias).

eliminations.label: Muscle dystrophin - Duchenne/Becker (your pick)
eliminations.detail: WHAT IT IS: dystrophin defects cause Duchenne/Becker muscular dystrophy (X-linked). ❌ WHY IT FAILS: those present with PROXIMAL weakness, calf PSEUDOHYPERTROPHY, and a waddling gait - not distal atrophy with pes cavus, areflexia, and sensory loss. Also, sensory loss and areflexia point to a NEUROPATHY, not a myopathy. ✅ Correct if: proximal weakness + calf pseudohypertrophy + high CK in a boy.

eliminations.label: Ryanodine receptors - malignant hyperthermia
eliminations.detail: WHAT IT IS: RYR1 mutations cause malignant hyperthermia (uncontrolled Ca release with volatile anesthetics/succinylcholine). ❌ WHY IT FAILS: this is an anesthetic-triggered hypermetabolic crisis, not a chronic hereditary neuropathy. ✅ Correct if: intraoperative rigidity, hyperthermia, hypercarbia.

eliminations.label: Synaptic vesicles - botulism/NMJ
eliminations.detail: WHAT IT IS: botulinum toxin cleaves SNARE proteins, blocking acetylcholine vesicle release. ❌ WHY IT FAILS: it causes acute descending flaccid paralysis with cranial nerve involvement, not a slowly progressive inherited neuropathy with pes cavus. ✅ Correct if: acute descending paralysis after canned food or in an infant given honey.

eliminations.label: Tau protein - neurodegenerative dementias
eliminations.detail: WHAT IT IS: hyperphosphorylated tau accumulates in Alzheimer and frontotemporal dementia. ❌ WHY IT FAILS: these are CNS dementias of older adults, not a peripheral neuropathy in a teenager. ✅ Correct if: progressive cognitive decline with neurofibrillary tangles.

reasoning: Distal atrophy + pes cavus + areflexia + sensory loss with an affected parent = hereditary peripheral neuropathy
This is Charcot-Marie-Tooth disease (autosomal dominant, onset in adolescence)
Most common subtype (CMT1) is caused by defective peripheral myelin protein (PMP22)
mechanism: Charcot-Marie-Tooth disease (CMT) is the most common group of hereditary peripheral neuropathies. The classic and most common subtype, CMT1, is a demyelinating neuropathy caused by an autosomal dominant duplication/mutation of the PMP22 gene, which encodes peripheral MYELIN PROTEIN 22 (other subtypes involve axonal proteins). Defective myelin slows nerve conduction and causes length-dependent degeneration of the longest peripheral nerves first, so patients present in adolescence with distal, symmetric muscle wasting and weakness (feet and legs, later hands), frequent ankle sprains, foot deformities (pes cavus, hammertoes), absent ankle reflexes, and distal sensory loss (vibration/proprioception). A family history in a parent affected at a similar age reflects the dominant inheritance. The distractors correspond to entirely different diseases: dystrophin (muscular dystrophy - proximal, pseudohypertrophy), ryanodine receptor (malignant hyperthermia), synaptic-vesicle/SNARE (botulism), and tau (Alzheimer/frontotemporal dementia).

difficulty.label: 🧠 Knowledge
difficulty.text: First Aid Neuro > Charcot-Marie-Tooth: hereditary peripheral neuropathy, autosomal dominant, PMP22 (CMT1) defective myelin; distal atrophy, pes cavus, areflexia, sensory loss.

difficulty.label: 📖 Comprehension
difficulty.text: Sensory loss + areflexia flag a NEUROPATHY (not a myopathy), and the dominant, distal, foot-deformity picture = CMT (myelin protein).

difficulty.label: 🔤 Vocab
difficulty.text: Unsure on pes cavus, areflexia, length-dependent neuropathy, PMP22, or demyelinating vs axonal? Tell me which.

difficulty.label: 🨤 Distractor
difficulty.text: Dystrophin = muscular dystrophy (proximal, pseudohypertrophy, no sensory loss); ryanodine = malignant hyperthermia; SNARE = botulism; tau = dementia.

difficulty.label: 🗒️ Other
difficulty.text: Bank: CMT = autosomal dominant hereditary neuropathy, PMP22 myelin defect; pes cavus + areflexia + distal atrophy.

memoryHook: Bad myelin (PMP22) in the longest nerves gives a teen high-arched feet, floppy ankles, and dead reflexes - Charcot-Marie-Tooth runs in the family.
